title: Twelve days
hookLine: Christmas runs from the 25th to Epiphany and beyond

lines: THE WISE MEN ARE ON THE BOOKCASE.
cards: On a shelf in a living room, a nativity set. The shepherds are already at the manger, but the wise men aren't. They're on the far side of the room, on top of the bookcase, camels and all.

Every morning someone moves them a little closer: across the bookcase, onto the windowsill, along the top of the piano. The rest of the street has dragged its trees to the curb, and these figures are still traveling.
They won't reach the manger until the Epiphany. The house is in no hurry, because the feast isn't over.

teach.h: THE WISE MEN WALK ACROSS THE ROOM.
teach.b: The twelve days run from Christmas to the Epiphany, the feast of the wise men, which you met in your first year. They come after Christmas, not before it.
The shops count down to the day; the Church counts forward from it. And in the Church's calendar the Christmas season runs on past the Epiphany, to the feast of the Baptism of the Lord.
Next, the walking wise men. Moving the figures a little each day is a home custom, not a law, but it makes the twelve days visible.
Matthew's Gospel says the wise men saw a star and came looking for the newborn king; in some homes they get there one bookshelf at a time.
Then, an odd thing: the day after Christmas, the Church keeps the feast of Stephen, a deacon stoned to death in Acts.
As the stones fall, the Douay-Rheims says: "And they stoned Stephen, invoking, and saying: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
Soon after come the Holy Innocents, the children of Bethlehem killed by Herod. Joy and grief share the same week; the Church doesn't keep grief away from the crib.
That's part of keeping the feast: celebrating with your eyes open. Last, the keeping.
Paul, calling Christ our Passover, tells the Corinthians to keep the feast with sincerity and truth instead of the old leaven of malice.

Keeping a feast is a choice made on ordinary days: lights left on in the window, someone invited over on a weekday, merry Christmas said when everyone else has moved on. Small, stubborn acts of celebration.

how: Catholics keep Christmas as a season, from Christmas Day through the Epiphany and on to the feast of the Baptism of the Lord. Some families keep the tree and crib up through those weeks, and some move the wise men figures closer to the manger each day until the Epiphany.

practice: Choose any feast that matters to you, Christmas, a birthday, an anniversary, a homecoming, and how fast it usually ends.

Then pick one small way to stretch it: a candle lit for another week, a card sent late on purpose, one more meal shared. If you pray, give thanks for the feast itself; if you don't, enjoy remembering it.

wordCard.voice: Twelve days. The days from Christmas to the Epiphany, with the Church's season running on to the Baptism of the Lord: a feast kept, not just a day marked. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the feast. Twelve days of it, and the season runs on. Same time tomorrow.
